sweep_summary: this search of works with stress in the title's single item, Pittman 1970 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies' (Hale & Pike Part II, pp. 1-8), was downloaded from the ERIC ED046002 microfiche scan on archive.org and read in full: it concerns the four register/pitch classes of monosyllabic word-bases and their consonant-voicing origin, mentions stress only for Tamang, and is silent on Gurung word-stress placement (priority none). As a by-product the Part I volume (ERIC ED046001, archive.org item micro_IA41153125_0126, mislabelled in IA metadata) yielded the published Glover 1970 'Gurung tone and higher levels' (pp. 52-73) whose 'Stress' section (p. 72) repeats verbatim the catalog's deciding passage (non-phonemic slight primary stress on the first syllable of the foot/word; secondary stress on the pitch-accented syllable), and Pike 1970 (p. 40) independently confirms initial demarcative stress with the contrastive-stress hypothesis rejected. catalog's classification fixed-strict initial is confirmed; no contradicting statement found. Glover & Glover 1972 'A guide to Gurung tone' remains unread (SIL: not online; HathiTrust search-only), low priority. discovery ran through archive.org, ERIC API, SIL archive pages (via the Internet Archive listing) and the HathiTrust volumes API (babel.hathitrust.org could not be reached by automated download). Everything downloaded is under and logged in there.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is not phonemic in Gurung--that is, it does not establish contrastive units (except for the presence of secondary stress on the accented syllable if in first or second position in the word, as described above). However the first syllable of a foot regularly carries a slight stress (primary by comparison with the secondary stress on the accented syllable), which serves as a characteristic feature distinguishing the foot, as a level, from the next lower, the syllable, and the next higher, the phonological phrase.

new_statements.reading: Fixed, non-contrastive, weak primary stress on the first syllable of the foot (= phonological word); the lexical high-pitch 'accent' can sit on any syllable and is a pitch contrast, not stress (it carries only a secondary stress when in 1st/2nd position). This is the published form of the very passage the catalog quotes from the 1969 SIL mimeo, so the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding stands; Pike 1970 (p. 40) independently reports the same initial demarcative stress and notes that a contrastive-stress hypothesis was tested and rejected.

sources.quote: Word stress is not phonemic in Gurung--that is, it does not establish contrastive units (except for the presence of secondary stress on the accented syllable if in first or second position in the word, as described above). However the first syllable of a foot regularly carries a slight stress (primary by comparison with the secondary stress on the accented syllable), which serves as a characteristic feature distinguishing the foot, as a level, from the next lower, the syllable, and the next higher, the phonological phrase. [...] In fact there is the primary stress on the first syllable and a decrescendo over the foot.

sources.quote: In Gurung the first syllable of a phonological word seems to be marked by an initial stress (in addition to the contrastive potentials for pitch and breathiness). This stress serves to help divide a phonological phrase into phonological words (or 'feet'). (Glover has tested our early hypothesis that stress may be contrastive throughout the word, but has now rejected this hypothesis.)

sources.quote: In this article he identified a clear prosody, which he, with the help of Deu Bahadur Gurung, who speaks that language, subdivided into 'intense' and 'relaxed', in contrast with a 'breathy' prosody, which they subdivided into 'rising' and 'low'. Thus every monosyllabic noun fell into one of four phonological classes. [...] the prosodies may be realized not only by pitch, voice quality and stress, but also by voicing versus voicelessness.
sources.locator: Part II p. 1 (p. 7), sec. 1, and p. 8 (p. 14), sec. 12
sources.note: 'Prosodies' here means the four register/pitch classes of monosyllabic word-bases (clear intense, clear relaxed, breathy rising, breathy low) and a hypothesis that they derive from initial/final consonant voicing (K/G) across Tamang-Gurung-Thakali, Sherpa and Chepang. The word 'stress' occurs only for Tamang (the Pike-Hale-Taylor 'three-tone, two-stress' analysis, p. 2) and generically on p. 8. Nothing on where word stress falls in Gurung.

sources.note: Gurung is widely acknowledged to be tonal but descriptions disagree on the categories; data from a Siklis speaker suggest word-initial obstruent voicing is phonemic in some dialects and that Siklis Gurung is best analysed with three tone categories - a low tone with breathy phonation, and high and mid tones with modal phonation - the three arising from a split of one of two proto-tones after loss of an initial voicing contrast; compared with earlier proposals (Glover, Burton-Page, Sprigg, Mazaudon).
